summary: Segment Routing over MPLS networks can span multiple IGP domains or autonomous systems under one organization. This document defines mechanisms for MPLS ping and traceroute in such inter-domain settings.

eli5.summary: When a delivery route crosses several regions, you still want to test it end to end. This extends the testing tools to work across regions.

questions: how does mpls traceroute work across autonomous systems
what is the reply path tlv
what are type-a type-c and type-d segment sub-tlvs
what does return code 0x0006 mean in mpls ping
subtitle: How to make MPLS ping and traceroute work across IGP domains and ASes, by telling each responder exactly how to send its reply back.

tldr.problem: LSP ping and traceroute need IP connectivity from each responding node back to the sender. On a Segment Routing path that crosses several ASes or IGP domains, that connectivity may not exist.
tldr.mechanism: The initiator uses Reply Mode 5 and puts a Reply Path TLV in the echo request. The TLV carries the return path as an ordered list of segments, using three new Segment sub-TLVs (Type-A, Type-C, Type-D). Border nodes can also build the return path step by step during traceroute.
tldr.outcome: Responders turn the segments into an MPLS label stack and send the echo reply as an ordinary labelled packet that any MPLS node can forward in the fast path. The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9716 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2025. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It covers SR-MPLS only and leaves the SRv6 data plane out of scope.

sections.title: The Inter-Domain Ping Problem
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) is a form of source routing, and it can be used with an MPLS data plane (SR-MPLS). A network may contain several IGP domains or several Autonomous Systems (ASes) under one organization. An end-to-end SR path can then cross all of them, for example by using BGP peering segments and Egress Peer Engineering SIDs (EPE-SIDs).

Operators want LSP ping and traceroute on such paths, to detect failed deliveries and to learn the path traffic really takes. The existing mechanisms (RFC 8029 and RFC 8287) send echo replies over IP. In an inter-AS network a responding node may have no IP route back to the source address of the ping, so the reply never arrives.

Earlier workarounds exist. RFC 8403 style monitoring could use GRE tunnels or static routes to every router, which the RFC calls operationally very heavy. The Echo-relay approach of RFC 7743 needs the return packet to be processed on the slow path or as a bump-in-the-wire on every relay node. This document offers an alternative that needs no change to the forwarding path.

In this document a domain is an IGP domain in which every node is visible to every other node for shortest path computation, meaning an IGP area or level. It covers both inter-area and inter-AS paths where the administrations are closely coordinating or under single ownership. The SRv6 data plane is out of scope.
sections.eli5: A helper far from home gets your message but cannot find the road back to you. The usual way to reply does not work between different regions, so this RFC gives the helper a better way to answer.

sections.title: The Reply Path TLV Approach
sections.content:
The idea reuses the Reply Path TLV from RFC 7110. The initiator sets the Reply Mode of the echo request to 5 (Reply via Specified Path) and includes a Reply Path TLV (TLV 21) that spells out the return path. In SR networks labels are assigned statically to nodes, so a head-end or Path Monitoring System (PMS) that knows the link-state database (LSDB) and the SIDs can build the reverse path by stacking segments.

Which segment types to send is a matter of local policy. Implementations may take labels, IPv4 addresses, IPv6 addresses or a mix as command-line input, or they may acquire the LSDB of remote domains and compute the return path. For traceroute the return path has to change as the trace crosses each domain, because the reply is sent from every node along the path.

The same procedures also apply to networks made of several IGP domains that use BGP Labeled Unicast (BGP-LU) or label stacking, with the domains joined at border routers. Networks made of IPv4-only and IPv6-only domains are out of scope; the RFC recommends dual-stack and end-to-end IPv6 addresses there.
sections.eli5: Instead of hoping the helper knows the way back, the sender writes the whole route home inside the message. The helper reads the route and follows it.

sections.title: The Segment Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
Three new sub-TLVs describe one segment each, and a Reply Path TLV can hold several, of mixed types. They are modelled on the segment types of RFC 9256. Their code points come from the registry shared by TLV types 1, 16 and 21, and this document defines their processing only inside TLV 21. If they show up in TLV 1 or 16, the responder MUST return an appropriate error code as defined in RFC 8029.

  • Type-A (sub-type 46): a SID only, in the form of an MPLS label. It is 8 bytes of value (Length 8) and holds Flags, a Label of 20 bits, a 3-bit TC, a reserved S bit and an 8-bit TTL. TC set to zero and TTL set to 255 mean the receiver may choose those values.
  • Type-C (sub-type 47): an IPv4 node address, an SR Algorithm and an optional SID. Length is 8 without the SID and 12 with it.
  • Type-D (sub-type 48): the same for an IPv6 node address. Length is 20 without the SID and 24 with it.

For Type-C and Type-D the node address MUST be present and should be a stable address such as a loopback. If the SID field is present it MUST be used to build the reply. Otherwise the responder derives the label from the Node-SID for that address using its own SRGB.

The Flags octet has one defined bit, the A-Flag, which says an SR Algorithm ID is present in the SR Algorithm field (a Segment Routing algorithm or a Flexible Algorithm). It applies to Type-C and Type-D and is ignored in Type-A. Reserved and unused bits MUST be zero on sending and ignored on receipt.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to write one step of the route: as a ready-made label number, or as the name of a router in IPv4 or IPv6 form so the reader can look up the label itself.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Echo Messages
sections.content:
The initiator starts the ping or traceroute, the responder answers an echo request, and the egress is the last node. To ping, the initiator MUST set Reply Mode to 5 and MUST include a Reply Path TLV holding the reverse SR path as an ordered list of segments. The first segment MUST be the top label the responder uses when it sends the reply.

A responder that gets Reply Mode 5 without a Reply Path TLV treats the request as malformed. If it does not support Reply Mode 5, or the request has a malformed Segment sub-TLV such as a wrong length, it sends an echo reply with Return Code "Malformed echo request received" and Subcode zero. Otherwise it performs the normal FEC validation of RFC 8029 and RFC 8287, unchanged, and uses the Reply Path TLV to build the reply.

The echo reply is an MPLS packet. Its top label MUST come from the first segment, the remaining labels follow the order of the TLV, and the responder MUST NOT add any other label. The S bit is set on the bottom label. The responder MAY check that the top label is reachable in its LFIB and, if not, SHOULD send the proper Return Code per RFC 7110. If the responder has no IP reachability to the originator the reply might not arrive at all, and the node MAY log this.

When the head-end could only supply Type-C or Type-D segments, the replying node MUST derive labels from the Node-SIDs for those addresses. If a given SID does not match the address in the segment, log information should be generated.
sections.eli5: The sender writes the route home in the message. The helper checks the message makes sense, then sends its answer along exactly that route and adds no extra stops.

sections.title: Building the Return Path Dynamically
sections.content:
A head-end may not see the whole inter-domain topology. In that case routers on the path can help build the return path during traceroute. The RFC defines a new Return Code for the Reply Path TLV, 0x0006, meaning "Use Reply Path TLV from this echo reply for building the next echo request". When the initiator receives it, it sends that Reply Path TLV in the next echo request with the TTL incremented by 1. If the TTL is already 255 the traceroute MUST end with a log message.

Who adds what depends on the node:

  • ABR: if local policy allows, it adds its own node label in front of any existing segments in the Reply Path TLV it returns. If the SRGB is not uniform it is RECOMMENDED to use a Type-C or Type-D segment. An existing Type-C or Type-D segment is converted to Type-A using the ABR's own SRGB.
  • ASBR receiving from another AS: it returns a Reply Path TLV with two segments, its own Node-SID on top and below it the EPE-SID back toward the AS the request came from, and sets Return Code 0x0006. Each further ASBR adds its Node-SID and EPE-SID on top of what is already there.
  • ASBR receiving from the same AS: it MUST convert any Type-C or Type-D segment to Type-A using its own SRGB and set 0x0006.
  • Internal nodes: they might not set 0x0006 because the return path does not change, so the initiator keeps sending the previous Reply Path TLV.

An ASBR whose local policy forbids taking part MUST return Return Code 0x0007, "Local policy does not allow dynamic return path building", and the dynamic procedure then fails. The initiator should log it, and the operator may specify the return path explicitly. Whatever segment types are used, a responder MUST always translate the Reply Path TLV into a label stack for the reply.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the sender does not know the whole map. So at each border crossing, the guard there adds a few directions home to the note, and the sender uses the longer note for the next question.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The appendix uses a topology of three ASes (AS1, AS2, AS3) joined by ASBRs, with PE1 in AS1 and PE4 in AS2. The path is the label stack [N-P1, N-ASBR1, EPE-ASBR1-ASBR4, N-PE4]. For a ping, PE1 puts a Reply Path TLV such as [N-ASBR4, EPE-ASBR4-ASBR1, N-PE1] in the request. PE4 validates the FEC, copies those labels into its reply and the reply is steered back to PE1. An implementation may also supply only labels that reach its own AS, in which case the exposed echo reply is forwarded by an IP lookup.

For traceroute with a head-end that knows the LSDB, PE1 first sends only its own node label as the return path. Once the trace reaches the AS border, the return path grows: after ASBR1 it becomes [EPE-ASBR4-ASBR1, N-PE1], and after ASBR4 it becomes [N-ASBR4, EPE-ASBR4-ASBR1, N-PE1]. When P3 has no route to N-PE4, the trace reaches P3 with TTL 5, P3 replies, and the next request with TTL 6 is dropped at P3. The trace therefore shows the path is broken at P3.

If SRGBs differ, the head-end sends a Type-C or Type-D segment for the top entry and a Type-A segment (using the SRGB of the border node) once the trace has crossed a border, because nodes beyond it cannot derive the right SRGB. A Type-C segment with the A-Flag and an algorithm value gives an algorithm-specific return path. The appendix also extends the idea to three ASes and to a single-border multi-area case with ABR1 and ABR2, where the return path holds one border node label per border.
sections.eli5: In the worked example a message travels across two regions. At each border the sender adds more directions home. When one road is missing, the last helper who answered shows exactly where the route breaks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The procedures are meant for domains under the same administration or closely cooperating administrations, and the RFC assumes that sharing domain-internal information among them is not a security risk. It also warns that an attacker could use the procedures to extract the domain's internal information.

Operators MUST deploy the filter policies of RFC 8029 to restrict LSP ping and traceroute packets by origin, and appropriate filters SHOULD be applied at the edges. It is RECOMMENDED to use mechanisms such as MACsec on inter-domain or otherwise vulnerable links to prevent spoofing. All the security considerations of RFC 8029 apply, including the need for mechanisms that prevent denial-of-service attacks.
sections.eli5: The note tells outsiders how your network is laid out, so only let trusted neighbours send these test messages and lock the doors at the edges.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned three sub-types from the "Sub-TLVs for TLV Types 1, 16, and 21" registry: 46 (Type-A), 47 (Type-C) and 48 (Type-D), in the Standards Action range (0-16383). IANA also created a new "Segment ID Sub-TLV Flags" registry for the 8 flag bits of the Flags field, numbered from 0 as the most significant bit, with new entries by Standards Action. Its first entry is the A-Flag.

Two Return Codes were added to the "Reply Path Return Codes" registry, 0x0006 and 0x0007, in the Standards Action range (0x0000-0xFFFB).
sections.eli5: Official number lists were updated so everyone uses the same numbers for the new message pieces and answer codes.

fields.desc: Zero on sending, ignored on receipt.

fields.desc: Traffic Class; zero lets the receiver choose.

fields.desc: Reserved; zero on sending, ignored on receipt.
